title: NovaInsights x Redwood - Customer Podcast Interview
summary: Recorded a ~42 minute customer interview/podcast with NovaInsights about their use of Redwood Inference for product personalization and search. Discussion covered business impact, a couple of concrete metrics (latency improvements, cost savings), a quick technical overview, and quotes for a case study. Agreed next steps: share edited audio, supply quotes + logo, draft case study for approval.
topics: High-level technical architecture (hosting and dedicated decisions)
Next steps: assets, approvals, publish timeline
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-06 16:00 UTC | Duration: 42m | Attendees: Elena (Redwood), Maya (Redwood), Michael (NovaInsights), Priya (NovaInsights), Jared (NovaInsights)

[00:00] Elena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, super excited to have NovaInsights on the podcast today. Quick mic check — can you hear me okay?
[00:10] Michael (NovaInsights): Yep, loud and clear. Thanks for having us.
[00:15] Maya (Redwood): Hi all, quick note — we'll record and share an edited clip. If there's anything you want us to skip just flag it.
[00:22] Priya (NovaInsights): Sounds good. We're excited to share some of the results we've seen.
[00:30] Elena: Great. So to kick off, Michael maybe give a quick intro to NovaInsights and the problem you were solving before Redwood.
[00:40] Michael: Sure. NovaInsights builds a B2B analytics product — think search and recommendation inside our app. Historically our search relied on a mix of rules and a lightweight vector store built with an in-house embedder. Latency was okay but quality suffered and costs were spiky when traffic peaked. We started evaluating LLM-based reranking and personalized prompts late 2024.
[01:05] Jared (NovaInsights): Yeah and marketing wanted better contextual recommendations for the trial funnel, so we had a product+marketing requirement to improve conversion without huge infra ops.
[01:20] Elena: Nice. Can you call out the timeline of adoption? When'd you go from POC to production?
[01:26] Michael: POC started January 2025, small sandbox with Redwood hosted API — we liked the onboarding and the latency SLOs you had docs for. By May 2025 we moved the reranking path to Dedicated capacity — that gave predictable throughput for our peak windows.
[01:45] Maya: When you moved to Dedicated did you change model families or quantization?
[01:50] Michael: We kept a curated open model — a 7B variant — and applied the 4-bit quantization profile suggested in Redwood Optimize. We saw about 2.4x cost reduction versus the non-quantized baseline and tail latency stayed under our 300ms SLO for 95th pctl which was big.
[02:17] Priya: To add, the auto-batching and prefix caching you guys had in the runtime cut our per-request cost further — that was a surprise benefit.
[02:30] Elena: Love that — those are great soundbites. Can you share a concrete metric around conversion lift or revenue impact?
[02:39] Michael: Sure — in the trial onboarding funnel we saw a 12% lift in activation rate attributed to the personalized suggestions powered by the reranker. That was measured via A/B over 6 weeks. For revenue, it's an estimated $120k ARR uplift in the first year of rollout.
[03:00] Jared: And ops time dropped too, like we no longer needed to tune many hand-crafted rules, saving an estimated 0.5 FTE worth of time monthly.
[03:12] Maya: Nice. From the product angle — any feedback on reliability or issues you hit early on?
[03:18] Michael: A couple of things — first, we did a deeper security review early because of PII concerns. Redwood's SOC 2 docs and KMS integration checks helped speed legal signoff. Second, we had one incident where a config rollout caused a brief spike in latency — the tracing dashboard in Redwood Console made troubleshooting quick.
[03:45] Priya: That incident was a good example of the rollback feature — we hit the automatic fallback to the hosted smaller model which kept the UI responsive.
[03:55] Elena: Perfect. Good quote there about rollback and graceful degradation.
[04:00] Elena: Let's pivot a bit to the technical side — for listeners who like the nerdy bits, can you describe the high-level infra diagram?
[04:08] Michael: Sure. Request path is frontend -> internal API -> Redwood route -> Dedicated pool. We use token-based auth and a VPC peering setup (for our private deployment we had a peering link). We also use Redwood's KV prefix cache for repeated user prefixes — that's reduced compute by a lot.
[04:30] Maya: Did you consider on-prem or hybrid?
[04:33] Michael: We evaluated Private on-prem for regulated customers but decided Dedicated in cloud with VPC and KMS was the best tradeoff for time-to-market.
[04:45] Elena: Good. Any specific integrations that were painful or pleasantly easy?
[04:49] Priya: SSO setup took a short run but documented steps were clear. The SDKs had a small breaking change mid-2025 but support helped us patch quickly.
[05:05] Jared: For marketing listeners, what's one or two user stories that really stuck out?
[05:11] Michael: One was the new trial guided tour — we used short context-aware prompts to shape suggestions; the onboarding completion jumped and people spent more time in higher-value features.
[05:25] Priya: Another was search within long technical docs where the reranker improved relevance for niche queries — that reduced support tickets by ~8% in a subset.
[05:38] Elena: Love those. Maybe let's capture a short, punchy quote for social: "Redwood cut our latency and let us focus on product, not infra." Would you be comfortable with that as a pull quote?
[05:49] Michael: Yeah, that's fine, maybe: "Redwood let us focus on product, not inference ops."
[05:56] Maya: Great. We'll include that as a lead quote.
[06:00] Elena: For the record, can you give one sentence on why you chose Redwood over building in-house or using other hosted providers?
[06:09] Michael: Two things — predictable performance with Dedicated and clear cost controls; and the quality of observability in the Console which meant our engineers could triage without deep infra work.
[06:22] Priya: Also the onboarding speed — we had a working POC in two weeks which was a big factor.
[06:30] Elena: Cool. We're getting great soundbites. Let's move to logistical items: approvals and assets. We'll need a headshot, company logo in svg, three brief pull quotes, and confirmation on publishing window.
[06:44] Jared: We can get the logo and headshot today. Pull quotes — Michael and Priya will pick two each.
[06:52] Elena: Awesome. We'll aim to send the first draft of the case study copy by 2026-03-12.
[06:58] Michael: That timeline works.
[07:02] Maya: Quick note for listeners: we'll redact any customer-only metrics if needed.
[07:08] Michael: Understood.
[07:10] Elena: Any funny stories or unexpected wins you want on mic?
[07:15] Michael: One week into the rollout we noticed anomalous traffic patterns — turned out a small cohort of power users were building custom dashboards and the system responded well; we discovered new upsell motion. That was a surprise.
[07:30] Priya: Also the support reduction — we internalized a few feature asks as product improvements rather than emergency tickets.
[07:38] Elena: Those are great. Listener-friendly anecdote.
[07:42] [Small crosstalk and laughter]
[08:00] Elena: I'm going to ask a couple of rapid-fire questions for the case study: worst thing that happened? Best decision you made?
[08:07] Michael: Worst — we underestimated the prefix cache warmup on day one, caused slower cold-starts; Best decision — move critical paths to Dedicated early so we could iterate on prompt design without noisy infra.
[08:25] Priya: Best decision — keep product and marketing closely aligned on prompt KPIs.
[08:30] Maya: Nice. Okay, for the editorial voice — are there any phrases or JDAs we should avoid? Any compliance language?
[08:38] Michael: Avoid specific customer names or PII; otherwise we're good.
[08:42] Elena: Great. We'll share a release plan and obtain sign-off before publishing.
[08:48] [Timestamp jump, mid-interview]);
[20:05] Elena: Quick edit note — we'll probably cut the deep technical bit for the public podcast and publish an extended tech appendix for the blog.
[20:15] Michael: That works. Devs appreciated the technical appendix.
[20:22] Maya: Final production questions — do you want the clip to be 2-3 minutes or longer?
[20:28] Jared: Keep it to 2 1/2 minutes for social, and we'll amplify on our channels.
[20:35] Elena: Great. We'll also produce a 30s soundbite for paid ads.
[20:40] Priya: Please include the conversion stat — it's a great hook.
[20:44] Elena: Noted.
[20:47] [Noise of sandwich wrapper off mic; brief laugh]
[25:00] Elena: Before we close, any blockers from legal or product?
[25:07] Michael: Legal asked for the list of metrics we'll publish; we'll send that by end of day.
[25:13] Priya: Product wants one more look at the wording for the conversion uplift before it's final.
[25:20] Elena: Okay we'll send the draft copy and highlight the pull quotes.
[25:25] Michael: Also, on a technical note, can we have the routing policy text — the snippet that describes Dedicated vs Hosted — to include in the appendix?
[25:33] Maya: Yes we'll send a short explainer doc.
[25:37] Elena: Perfect.
[25:40] [Small chatter; audio edit cue]
[30:00] Elena: Alright folks this has been super helpful. Any last-minute requests?
[30:07] Michael: No, just a quick ask — please include the 12% activation stat with the context of the A/B test size.
[30:14] Elena: We'll do that.
[30:18] Priya: Thanks for putting this together.
[30:20] Jared: Thanks everyone.
[30:22] Elena: Okay, we'll wrap and circle on the next steps. Thanks again for being on the show.
[30:30] [Meeting ends — informal signoff and small audio chatter]

Notes: transcription has occasional imperfections (proper names and product names may be slightly off), edited for brevity in parts.
